input: Phase equilibrium is a truly fundamental concept in thermodynamics, and nowhere is it more richly illustrated than in the familiar phenomenon of boiling. When a pure liquid is heated at a constant pressure, its temperature rises steadily at first, but once boiling commences something remarkable happens: the temperature simply stops rising, and all of the heat that continues to be supplied is consumed in converting liquid into vapour instead. The condition that governs this behaviour is the equality of the chemical potential of the substance in the two phases, which is to say that the chemical potential of the liquid and the chemical potential of the vapour are exactly the same at equilibrium, and it is this equality, expressed in words, that defines the boiling point before any equation is brought into play. If the chemical potential in the liquid were higher, molecules would pass into the vapour; if it were lower, vapour would condense, and in either case the system would keep changing until the two values came into balance. Boiling, then, is not merely the appearance of bubbles, picturesque as that may be: it is the visible signature of two phases coexisting in equilibrium, with molecules crossing the interface continuously in both directions at equal rates. This is also why the temperature remains pinned throughout the process, because any heat added at the boiling point shifts the balance of amounts between the phases rather than raising the temperature of either one, and the equilibrium condition itself depends only on temperature and pressure, not on how much of each phase happens to be present.
target: A pure component boils at a fixed temperature when the surrounding pressure is held constant, and heat supplied during boiling changes the amounts of the two phases, not the temperature. The equilibrium condition is stated in words first: at equilibrium, the chemical potential of the component in the liquid equals its chemical potential in the vapour. Chemical potential measures the tendency of the component to leave the phase it is in. Where the liquid value stands higher, material passes into the vapour; where the vapour value stands higher, material condenses. Transfer stops, on balance, only where the two values are equal, although molecules continue to cross the interface in both directions at equal rates. The boiling point is the temperature at which the equality holds under the imposed pressure. A rise in pressure moves the boiling point upward, because the equality is restored at a higher temperature; a fall in pressure moves the boiling point down by the same mechanism. During boiling itself, neither temperature nor pressure changes while both phases remain present. Heat added in this state converts liquid to vapour at the equilibrium temperature, and heat removed condenses vapour, so the phase amounts absorb the energy change that would otherwise appear as a temperature change. The condition depends on temperature and pressure alone, and not on the relative amounts of liquid and vapour in the vessel. It holds for a pure component; a mixture, whose composition changes as boiling proceeds, does not boil at one fixed temperature.
